extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, publishers, researchers and research-integrity stakeholders concerned with peer-review processes
extracted.subtask_description: Practices and policy guidance for journals and publishers to prevent fake or compromised peer review, covering reviewer selection/verification, editorial oversight, transparency, third‑party services, and contractual/publisher-level safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict policies on suggested/recommended reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement strict policies on the use of suggested or recommended reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Springer/SAGE: 'implementing strict policies on the use of suggested or recommended reviewers...' Commenters: 'journals should stop asking authors to recommend potential reviewers and let the editors decide whom to contact.' Anti-pattern: relying on author-supplied reviewer contacts without independent verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require and verify institutional email addresses for reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Require the use and supply of institutional email addresses for reviewers and verify reviewer contact details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Springer/SAGE statement: '...the use and supply of institutional email addresses.' Commenters: 'journals should use the web and find that info themselves.' This prevents acceptance of fabricated reviewer emails that route to bogus accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manual screening and investigation of reviewer lists and past reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Conduct extra/manual screening and deeper investigations of reviewer names and review records to detect fabricated or compromised reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Springer: 'Based on this extra screening, new names of fake reviewers were detected' and 'The current retractions ... are the result of a deeper manual investigation.' Practice: periodic audits of past peer-review records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors independently recruit reviewers (use literature/web searches)
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should identify and recruit reviewers themselves (e.g., via PubMed or web searches) rather than relying primarily on author suggestions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From a practising editor: 'I try to avoid using the reviewers recommended by the authors, instead I do a pubmed and a google search to find potential reviewers.' Guidance: verify expertise and independence by checking publications and affiliations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check for conflicts of interest and collaborations before inviting reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify that potential reviewers are not collaborators or have conflicts of interest with the authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comment: 'There are rules to follow (not a collaborator, etc.)' and 'I would check if the authors had collaborated with the potential reviewers.' Anti-pattern: appointing close collaborators or competitors who have conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain larger reviewer pools and require multiple independent reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Build a pool of experts (e.g., identify 7–10 potential reviewers) and require several independent review reports (e.g., decisions based on any 3 independent reviews).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed workflow: 'find 7-10 experts... Once they get the review report from any 3 of these reviewers, they can take the decision based on that.' Benefit: reduces dependence on any single reviewer and makes manipulation harder.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build and share vetted reviewer databases
rubrics_metrics.description: Compile and share databases of reviewers who provide high-quality, reliable reviews across journals/publishers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested: 'each journal can build up a data base of the reviewers who do good reviewers and share this database among the journals/publishers.' Helps editors identify trustworthy reviewers quickly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blacklist or sanction actors who publish in/operate bogus journals or commit fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and block authors or actors involved with bogus journals or fraudulent activity from submission or reviewer roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggestion: 'Blacklist all the authors who publish in bogus journals and reject the paper submission by such authors without any review.' Note: contentious; implementation raises fairness and due-process concerns and may require institutional investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate and set policies on third‑party editing or submission services
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine links between authors and third-party editing/submission services that might supply fabricated reviews; create policies to manage/ban such services or require disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Article note: 'Some of the authors may have used a third-party editing service, which may have supplied the reviews.' Comment: 'I hope somebody will look into the possible link to an editing company — and, crucially, whether the authors were aware...' Practice: institutional investigations to establish intent and consequences (resubmission if authors were duped).

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow COPE and other best-practice guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt and share detailed guidance on best practice in line with COPE guidelines for peer review and research integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SAGE: 'regularly share detailed guidance on best practice in line with COPE guidelines.' Use COPE flowcharts and recommendations for investigating peer-review manipulation and retraction decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overhaul peer-review processes and editorial boards when relaunching journals
rubrics_metrics.description: When publishing changes hands or relaunching, restructure the editorial board and overhaul peer-review processes to align with publisher standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SAGE: 'the editorial board would be re-structured and there would be a complete overhaul of the peer review processes of the journal to bring it in line with SAGE practices.' Practical steps include new reviewer verification steps, updated policies, and training for editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publisher-level due diligence on society/business relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers should regularly review relationships with business partners and societies and be prepared to end contracts if integrity risks persist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Springer: 'Springer reviews on a regular basis all relationships with its business partners. The contract ... has been discontinued and not renewed.' Publisher oversight can be a lever for enforcement of standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance anonymity vs. accountability (do not force reviewer signatures uncritically)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be cautious about mandating signed/open reviews; forcing reviewers to sign can reduce willingness to review and may harm review supply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comment: 'Please please please no forcing people to sign reviews! ... I would simply stop reviewing if I had to sign everything I had to say.' Policy should balance transparency with reviewer safety and willingness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require declarations of interest and consider signed declarations for reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Require reviewers to disclose conflicts of interest; some propose signed statutory declarations to deter fraud (weigh costs/benefits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggestion: 'How about statutory declarations by peer reviewers – signed' (rebuttal: 'extra paperwork for the honest; no deterrent to the dishonest'). Consider non-onerous but enforceable COI disclosure mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude reviewers who are direct competitors or have adversarial motives
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid appointing reviewers who are in direct competition with the authors or who might act vindictively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From commentary: '“Reviewers” who are in competition with authors have a conflict of interest.' Also: '“Reviewers” should not be vindictive just because authors have not referenced their work.' Screening for professional competition is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer conduct standards: constructive, not vindictive criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Encourage reviewers to provide constructive feedback and avoid ad hominem or unduly negative comments; if a reviewer has nothing positive to add, be cautious about unnecessarily destructive reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice: 'If “Reviewers” have nothing positive to contribute, try not to say negative things — it may not suit your taste, but it does not mean the paper is no good.' Include editorial oversight to filter abusive reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify reviewer identity via institutional directories/publication records
rubrics_metrics.description: Confirm reviewer identities and contact details by cross-checking institutional directories and publication records rather than relying on author-supplied contact info.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters: 'journals should use the web and find that info themselves. I don’t know of any university that doesn’t post a directory.' This is a practical verification step to prevent fake-email scams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow re-submission if authors were unknowingly duped by third parties
rubrics_metrics.description: Where investigations show authors were deceived by third parties (e.g., editing services), permit re-submission after appropriate investigation and remediation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liz Wager: 'if the authors were duped they should be allowed to re-submit their work.' Requires careful institutional investigation to establish whether authors acted in bad faith.
